nameStory: Black swallow-wort gets its dark name from its deep purple-black flowers that stand out against summer's greenery. The 'swallow-wort' part comes from an old belief that these plants could cure diseases in swallows and other birds, though there's no truth to this folk remedy.
description: Black swallow-wort is a climbing vine that can grow 3-6 feet tall, twining around other plants and fences with its flexible stems. It produces clusters of small, star-shaped flowers that are so dark purple they appear almost black from a distance. The leaves are heart-shaped and grow in opposite pairs along the stem, giving the vine a neat, organized appearance as it scrambles over whatever it can find to climb.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small star-shaped flowers in clusters, so dark purple they look nearly black, with five pointed petals that feel waxy to the touch and have an unpleasant smell when crushed

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs, smooth-edged with a slightly glossy surface and prominent veining, turning yellow in fall

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Twining vine that climbs by wrapping its stems clockwise around supports, reaching 3-6 feet tall and forming dense tangles

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Slender seed pods about 2-4 inches long that split open to release seeds with silky white hairs that catch the wind like tiny parachutes

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, green to reddish stems that feel firm and slightly rubbery, releasing a milky sap when broken that may irritate sensitive skin

habitat: Black swallow-wort thrives in disturbed areas like roadsides, field edges, and abandoned lots, particularly in areas with rich, well-drained soil. You'll often find it climbing over fences, shrubs, and other plants in both sunny and partially shaded locations. It's becoming increasingly common in suburban areas and along transportation corridors throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge in late spring, with heart-shaped leaves unfurling in opposite pairs as the vine begins its climbing growth.
seasonality.summer: The distinctive dark purple-black flowers bloom from June through August, arranged in small clusters along the stems.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow before dropping, while long, slender seed pods develop and eventually split open to release fluffy seeds.
seasonality.winter: The vine dies back to the ground, leaving only dried stems and scattered seed pods as evidence of its presence.

funFact: This European invader is so successful at taking over native plant communities that it can reduce the food available to monarch butterfly caterpillars, even though monarchs sometimes mistake it for milkweed and lay eggs on it—but the caterpillars can't survive on this imposter!
confusionNotes: Black swallow-wort is often confused with native milkweeds because of its similar seed pods with fluffy seeds, but milkweeds have much lighter colored flowers (pink, orange, or white) and their leaves are usually alternate rather than opposite. Remember: black flowers and opposite leaves = invasive swallow-wort.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'dog-strangling vine,' this plant doesn't actually strangle dogs—the name comes from a literal translation of its scientific name and refers to its reputation for choking out other plants. It's actually part of the dogbane family, not related to true milkweeds despite the similar appearance of their seeds.
compareHints: Black swallow-wort differs from its close relative European swallow-wort primarily in flower color—European swallow-wort has cream-colored or pale yellow flowers instead of the dark purple-black ones. Both species have the same heart-shaped opposite leaves and climbing habit, so flower color is your best distinguishing feature between these two invasive vines.

relatedSpecies.distinction: European swallow-wort can be distinguished from its close relative black swallow-wort by its pale yellow-green flowers (black swallow-wort has dark purple to maroon flowers).
